title: The Lost Art of Manners and Why Children Still Need Them
author: Brenden Bott
summary: Brenden Bott, a classical Christian school head and parent, argues that manners are indispensable in raising and educating children, and that neglecting to train children in them harms the very people adults are called to form. He grounds the case in Scripture, reading Galatians 5:14 alongside the two greatest commandments to argue that love of God is displayed in concrete love of the neighbour in front of us, and uses Dostoyevsky's character who loves humanity but cannot stand people as a warning. His central move is to define manners as the outward forms of an inward care for others, which children do not learn naturally and must be taught. He anticipates the charge of legalism, answering that clear expectations of love actually expose the self-curved heart and point children to the gospel, while warning against Pharisaic pride. Finally he distinguishes basic courtesy from cultural 'manners' that demand affirmation or silence, and calls Christian families to a standard of kindness and generosity higher than mere politeness.
points: Bott defines manners as the outward forms of an inward care for others, making them a practical expression of the command to love one's neighbour.
He insists from experience as a parent and educator that children do not learn manners naturally, so they must be deliberately trained.
Answering the charge of legalism, he argues that clear standards of love help children see their own self-centredness and their need for the gospel.
He warns that some modern manners, such as affirming people in sin or staying silent, must be resisted because Christians are called to be good rather than merely nice.
Christian manners, in his account, go beyond recovered etiquette to hospitality, generosity, and love of enemies.
quotes: But whatever picture you may have in your mind, I want to suggest that manners are indispensable, especially in the education of children, and that the failure to train our children in them harms those we are called by God to teach.

It takes more than dreams of sacrifice about abstract people; real love is active in its response to the person in front of us. It is in our neighbour that our love for God is proved and fulfilled and our heart is given the opportunity to grow.

Now it is true that we can have good manners and hard hearts, but it is difficult to see how we can genuinely and regularly show care for others while ignoring manners. It is difficult to understand how we can be attentive in our love for others and not say "Please" when we ask for something and "Thank you" when we receive help or a gift.
As a parent and an educator, I can promise you this: children do not learn manners naturally.
Whenever we look down upon others because we do something that they do not do, we are no better than Pharisees and have twisted the intent of manners into something perverse and vain.

Though we want to be polite and always filled with grace when we speak, Christian manners must not require silence when there are serious temporal and eternal consequences at stake in a person's life due to his or her behaviour. We are called to be good rather than "nice" and always inoffensive.

Manners, at their best, are the cultural forms that we use to show others our love and care for them. Though there are times when manners may be distorted and some of their cultural expressions found wanting, they are essential to teach to our children, and we neglect them at our peril and theirs, as well as the common good.
